newsitem.title: FRANCE: NATO, France deny reported Franco-U.S. snub.
newsitem.headline: NATO, France deny reported Franco-U.S. snub.

text.p: NATO and France on Thursday flatly denied a report that French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette had snubbed retiring U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher by walking out of a toast in his honour at an alliance lunch.

In a statement issued by the French Foreign Ministry, NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said: "After we verified with participants at the lunch, I can state quite clearly and formally there is no substance to this story."

The Washington Post reported that de Charette had stood up and left the room while Solana was proposing a toast to the secretary of state at an alliance foreign ministers' meeting in Brussels on Wednesday.

It quoted an unnamed senior U.S. official as saying: "It was an incredible display of petulant behaviour. Everybody knows there are tensions in the French-American relationship, but nobody expects them to be shown at a personal level."
De Charette called the report a "manipulation" and his spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt branded it an "ill-intentioned lie".
The French minister told Reuters: "I cannot explain it. But I severely condemn this kind of manoeuvring because I do not doubt this was a manipulation."

Solana said there had been no toast, since Christopher had received a farewell tribute during the earlier ministerial working session, and de Charette had not left the dining room at any moment during the lunch.
Rummelhardt said he would demand that the Paris-based International Herald Tribune, which reprinted the Washington Post story, publish a correction.

Whatever actually occurred, the controversy reflects the raw state of Franco-U.S. relations, with disputes accumulating over the reform of NATO's military structure, the succession to U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, France's drive for a bigger say in the Middle East and Western policy on Zaire.

Paris and Washington frequently find themselves at odds on key global issues, but diplomats say Franco-American ties appear at a low ebbs despite a warm personal relationship between Presidents Bill Clinton and Jacques Chirac.
Probably the most serious fight concerns the future of NATO's southern command, which controls the Mediterranean.

In what has been dubbed the battle for Naples, France is demanding that Washington hand over the post it has held since NATO was created in 1949 to a European. The United States has flatly refused and is not amenable to compromise.

France says the U.S. Sixth Fleet, which comes under the same commander in Naples, could be placed under the direct control of the American Supreme Allied Commander in Europe (SACEUR), who is based in Mons, Belgium.
Another bitter and enduring dispute is over leadership of the United Nations. Paris had campaigned for the reappointment of Boutros-Ghali, vetoed by Washington.
The tables turned this week when the United States came out in favour of Ghanaian Kofi Annan to succeed Boutros-Ghali and France threatened to block his appointment.

There was apparently no progress at NATO on the southern command dispute. Paris has hinted that a U.S. refusal could halt its return to NATO's military structure, which it left 30 years ago, and possibly delay the alliance's plan to expand eastwards.

The investigative weekly Le Canard Enchaine reported last week that senior French officials considered ties with Washington to be in an "appalling" state but Chirac had ordered government officials to speak only in positive terms of the relationship.
